short: Price-to-earnings: what you pay for each rupee or dollar of yearly profit. The starting lens for cheap vs expensive.
definition: The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio divides a stock's price by its earnings per share over the last twelve months. A P/E of 20 means investors pay Rs 20 (or $20) for every Rs 1 ($1) of annual profit.

Rough landmarks: under ~15 is value territory, 15–25 is the broad-market norm, above ~30 prices in serious future growth. Always compare within a sector — a utility at 12x and software at 35x can both be fairly priced.
example: A stock at Rs 500 earning Rs 25 per share trades at 20x. If earnings double to Rs 50 and the price stays put, the P/E halves to 10x — the classic value-setup arithmetic.
inExtension: Every watchlist row shows P/E beside price, and the AI Verdict combines it with ROCE for a one-glance cheap-or-expensive call. Tap the column header to switch to Div Yld, ROCE, ROE or P/B.

faqs.q: Is a low P/E always a buy?
faqs.a: No — it can signal a bargain or a business in decline. Check earnings trend, debt and peers first.

faqs.q: Why do loss-making companies show no P/E?
faqs.a: Negative or zero earnings make the ratio meaningless. Use price-to-sales or cash-flow multiples instead.

short: Return on capital employed: how efficiently a company turns invested money into profit. Above 15–20% signals quality.
definition: ROCE (return on capital employed) measures operating profit against the total capital tied up in the business. It answers: for every Rs 100 invested in this company, how much operating profit comes back each year?
Sustained ROCE above 15–20% usually marks a genuine moat — pricing power, asset lightness or scale. Below ~10%, the business likely destroys value once its cost of capital is counted.
example: Two railway suppliers earn the same profit, but one uses half the factories and working capital. Its ROCE is double — and it can fund growth without borrowing.
inExtension: ROCE pairs with P/E to build the AI Verdict: cheap (low P/E) plus efficient (high ROCE) flags possible bargains; expensive plus weak ROCE flags risk.

faqs.q: ROCE vs ROE — what's the difference?
faqs.a: ROCE counts all capital including debt; ROE counts only shareholder equity. ROCE is harder to inflate with borrowing, so quality investors prefer it.

short: Return on equity: profit earned per rupee of shareholder money. High and stable ROE compounds wealth.
definition: ROE (return on equity) divides net profit by shareholder equity. A 20% ROE means each Rs 100 of shareholder funds generated Rs 20 of profit this year.
Read it with leverage in mind: heavy borrowing shrinks equity and flatters ROE. Pair it with ROCE and debt-to-equity before concluding a company is excellent.
example: A bank earning 1.2% on assets (ROA) with 8x leverage posts roughly 15%+ ROE — normal for banking, alarming anywhere else. Context decides.
inExtension: ROE is one tap away on the switchable ratio column — compare it across banks, IT and FMCG names without opening new tabs.

faqs.q: What is a good ROE?
faqs.a: Above 15% sustained over 5+ years is strong in most sectors; banks run higher on leverage, utilities lower on asset intensity. Trend beats level.

short: Price-to-book: market price versus net asset value per share. The classic yardstick for banks and asset-heavy firms.
definition: The price-to-book (P/B) ratio compares market price to book value per share (assets minus liabilities). A P/B of 2 means investors pay twice the accounting net worth.
It works best where book value is meaningful — banks, insurers, utilities. It misleads for asset-light software or brand businesses whose real value never sits on the balance sheet.
example: A bank trading at 1.2x book with 1%+ ROA is usually cheaper than a rival at 0.8x book hiding bad loans — asset quality adjusts every P/B reading.
inExtension: P/B auto-derives for Indian stocks so the column never shows blank, and formats Screener-style (2.4, not 2.40).

faqs.q: Is P/B under 1 always cheap?
faqs.a: Often it prices distress — bad loans, stranded assets or structural decline. Cheap on book still needs clean assets underneath.

short: Annual dividend divided by share price. A 4% yield pays Rs 4 yearly per Rs 100 invested — if the payout lasts.
definition: Dividend yield is yearly dividend per share divided by current price. It tells income investors what the stock pays them to wait.
High yield needs verification: divide by a crashed price and any dividend looks generous. Check payout ratio (under ~80%) and free-cash-flow cover before trusting yields above ~6%.
example: Coal India paying Rs 24 on a Rs 400 price yields 6%. If earnings cover it 1.5x from operating cash, the income thesis holds; if paid from debt, it does not.
inExtension: Div Yld sits on the switchable ratio column — scan an entire watchlist's income at a glance, then set price alerts at your target entry yields.

faqs.q: Are dividends taxed in India?
faqs.a: Yes, in the shareholder's hands at slab rates. Compare post-tax yield with debt options before choosing income stocks.

short: Price times shares outstanding: the market's price tag for the whole company. Defines large, mid and small caps.
definition: Market capitalisation is share price multiplied by total shares — what buying every share would cost. India broadly calls the top 100 large-caps, 101–250 mid-caps, the rest small-caps.
Size predicts behaviour: large-caps offer liquidity and stability, small-caps offer growth with gut-wrenching drawdowns. Most multibaggers start small; most frauds do too.
example: A Rs 50 stock with 100 crore shares (Rs 5,000 crore cap) is 'bigger' than a Rs 5,000 stock with 10 lakh shares (Rs 500 crore). Price per share alone says nothing about size.
inExtension: Market cap shows on every row and inside tape popups with sparkline, period returns and AI verdict — size context without leaving the page.

faqs.q: Large-cap vs small-cap — which returns more?
faqs.a: Small-caps have outperformed over long stretches with far deeper crashes. Match the cap to your stomach, not just your spreadsheet.

faqs.q: Can market cap change without price moving?
faqs.a: Yes — bonuses, splits, buybacks and fresh issuance all change share count. Watch corporate actions alongside price.

short: Earnings per share: the company's yearly profit divided by share count. The 'E' inside P/E.
definition: EPS (earnings per share) splits net profit across every share. Growing EPS is what ultimately drags stock prices upward over years.
Distinguish trailing EPS (last twelve months, factual) from forward EPS (analyst estimates, hopeful). P/E ratios built on forward EPS look cheaper by construction.
example: Profit of Rs 100 crore across 10 crore shares = Rs 10 EPS. At Rs 200, the P/E is 20x — now you see how the two metrics lock together.
inExtension: The tape popup's period-returns and P/E views both derive from earnings data — one click shows whether price or earnings moved faster.

faqs.q: Diluted vs basic EPS?
faqs.a: Diluted counts convertible options and warrants too — always use diluted for conservative valuation.

short: India's benchmark: 50 large stocks across 14+ sectors on the NSE. When India 'is up 1%', this is usually the number.
definition: The Nifty 50 tracks fifty large, liquid Indian stocks weighted by market value. Banks and IT dominate, so financial results season moves the index disproportionately.
Foreign investors benchmark India allocations to it, and derivatives on it are among the world's most traded — expiry-day swings often start here.
example: A 200-point Nifty move on HDFC Bank and Reliance earnings day can happen while most small-caps fall — index versus portfolio divergence is normal.
inExtension: The Markets tab opens economies with native indices and whole-market breadth (Nifty 500 advance/decline for India), so you see past the headline number.

faqs.q: Nifty vs Sensex — which to follow?
faqs.a: Both mirror India's large-caps and move together; Nifty (NSE, 50 stocks) leads derivatives, Sensex (BSE, 30 stocks) leads headlines. Either works as a benchmark.

short: BSE's 30-stock benchmark and India's oldest market barometer. Asia's first exchange, still the headline number.
definition: The Sensex tracks thirty large BSE-listed stocks. Launched in 1986, it remains the number TV tickers quote — even though professionals benchmark to the broader Nifty.
Same market, slightly narrower basket: expect near-identical long-run returns with marginally higher concentration.
example: 'Sensex crosses 80,000' headlines mark sentiment milestones — useful for gauging euphoria, useless for timing entries.
inExtension: Watch Indian benchmarks beside your holdings in the Markets tab, with macro tiles (inflation, GDP) for context behind the number.

faqs.q: Can I invest directly in the Sensex?
faqs.a: Via Sensex ETFs and index funds from multiple AMCs — compare expense ratio and tracking error first.

short: 500 large US companies, cap-weighted. The default scoreboard for American equities — and your global benchmark.
definition: The S&P 500 holds five hundred leading US companies chosen by committee for size, liquidity and profitability. Roughly a third of its weight sits in the Magnificent 7.
Most active US funds underperform it over a decade, which is why it anchors global portfolios — including those of Indian investors diversifying abroad.
example: When Nvidia reports, the S&P 500 often moves more on that one print than on the other 499 combined — concentration in action.
inExtension: The homepage tape and Markets tab track the S&P 500, Nasdaq and Dow live in dollars — open the extension on any tab to see them.

faqs.q: How can Indians invest in the S&P 500?
faqs.a: Feeder mutual funds, ETFs, or direct US-stock platforms under LRS limits. Compare fees, tracking error and tax treatment across routes.

short: The US tech-heavy exchange and its indices (Composite, Nasdaq 100). Growth's home — faster rallies, harder falls.
definition: Nasdaq is both an exchange and shorthand for its indices. The Composite covers 3,000+ stocks; the Nasdaq 100 holds the top 100 non-financials and underlies the QQQ ETF.
Tech concentration means rate sensitivity: when yields spike, long-duration growth valuations compress and Nasdaq leads declines.
example: A 1% Fed-surprise repricing often moves Nasdaq 2%+ while the Dow barely blinks — duration explains the gap.
inExtension: The Markets tab shows Nasdaq beside S&P 500 and Dow with whole-market NYSE + Nasdaq breadth, so narrow tech rallies can't fool you.

faqs.q: Nasdaq vs NYSE — what's the difference?
faqs.a: Two rival exchanges: Nasdaq is electronic and tech-heavy; NYSE hosts more old-economy giants. Listings, not quality, separate them.

short: Foreign vs domestic institutional investors. Their tug-of-war sets India's market tone — FIIs flee, DIIs absorb.
definition: FIIs (foreign institutional investors) now called FPIs, deploy global capital into India; DIIs (domestic institutions) — mutual funds, insurers, NPS — invest local savings. Daily buy/sell figures move sentiment more than fundamentals short-term.
The structural shift: monthly SIP flows made DIIs persistent buyers, cushioning FII exits that once crashed markets. Watch the net, not one side.
example: Rs 2.45 lakh crore of FPI outflows in a risk-off year were absorbed without a bear market — DII SIPs did the heavy lifting.
inExtension: When FII selling hits your watchlist, Smart Focus blue-dots the big movers so you triage damage in seconds.

faqs.q: Why do FII outflows crash small-caps most?
faqs.a: Foreign selling hits large-cap liquidity first, then sentiment and margin calls cascade down the market-cap ladder.

short: Exchange price bands that freeze trading after sharp moves — usually 2%, 5%, 10% or 20% per stock.
definition: Circuit breakers (price bands) cap how far a stock can move in a day. Hit the upper circuit and buyers queue with no sellers; hit lower and you cannot exit — the classic penny-stock trap.
Bands revise with volatility and corporate actions. Index-level market-wide halts (Nifty/Sensex ±10/15/20%) pause the whole market instead.
example: A 20% lower-circuit lock means your sell order sits unfilled all day while the quote blinks red — liquidity risk made visible.
inExtension: Price alerts notify you before extremes, and movement highlights flag threshold crosses the moment they happen.

faqs.q: Can circuits be revised mid-day?
faqs.a: Exchanges revise bands periodically; special pre-open sessions handle520%+ corporate-action adjustments. Check the day's applicable filter before trading.

short: CNN's 0–100 gauge of US market sentiment across seven inputs. Extreme fear often marks opportunity; extreme greed marks danger.
definition: The Fear & Greed Index blends seven signals — momentum, put/call ratios, volatility, safe-haven demand and more — into one 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed) reading for US stocks.
It is contrarian fuel, not a timer: extremes persist for weeks. Pair it with breadth and valuations before acting.
example: Readings under 20 have historically clustered near tradable bottoms; above 80, rallies keep working until breadth breaks — sentiment confirms, positioning decides.
inExtension: The Market Mood gauge shows the live CNN Fear & Greed value for the USA right above gainers, losers and breadth — hover the arc for its zone.

faqs.q: Does India have a Fear & Greed index?
faqs.a: Tickertape's Market Mood Index (MMI) plays that role — the extension shows it live for India. See Market Mood Index.

short: Tickertape's live 0–100 sentiment gauge for Indian stocks — the desi Fear & Greed, from extreme fear to extreme greed.
definition: The Market Mood Index compresses volatility, momentum and demand signals for Indian equities into a single live number. Under ~30 reads fear, above ~70 greed.
Like all sentiment tools it works best against the crowd: fear zones favour staggered buying quality, greed zones favour booking profits and tightening stops.
example: MMI under 20 during FII-selling panics has repeatedly marked zones where SIPs and staggered large-cap buys compounded well.
inExtension: The Market Mood gauge pulls the live Tickertape MMI for India (CNN Fear & Greed for the USA, data proxy elsewhere) — tap the info icon for the factors behind the number.

faqs.q: Is MMI a buy/sell signal?
faqs.a: No — a sentiment thermometer. Combine it with valuations, breadth and your asset allocation before acting.

short: Winners divided by losers across the market. Above 1 means broad gains; below 1, broad pain — breadth in one number.
definition: The advance-decline ratio divides rising stocks by falling ones. A 2:1 day means twice as many winners — healthy participation. A rising index with a sub-1 ratio means a few giants mask broad weakness.
Professionals distrust rallies the ratio doesn't confirm: narrow leadership breaks first when sentiment turns.
example: Nifty up 0.5% while the advance-decline reads 1:2 warns the headline is HDFC Bank and Reliance carrying 1,800 fallers — fragile, not strong.
inExtension: True whole-market breadth sits above gainers and losers: Nifty 500 totals for India, NYSE + Nasdaq for the USA — not partial counts.

faqs.q: Where do I see advance-decline data?
faqs.a: Moneycontrol (India) and WSJ Market Diary (US) publish it; the extension's Markets tab surfaces both with a 10-minute cache.

short: A stock's highest and lowest price over the past year. Breakouts signal strength; breakdowns signal trouble — both demand volume proof.
definition: The 52-week high/low frames today's price against a full year of trading. Stocks near highs carry momentum and overhead-supply tests; stocks near lows carry turnaround hopes or terminal decline.
New highs on rising volume confirm institutional accumulation; new lows on volume confirm distribution. Price alone, without volume, is half the story.
example: A railway stock breaking its 52-week high after a Rs 10,000-crore order win differs completely from one drifting to highs on thin volume — same price, opposite meaning.
inExtension: Smart Focus blue-dots stocks near 52-week extremes so they surface automatically; hit Focus to see only firing stocks.

faqs.q: Should I buy 52-week highs?
faqs.a: Momentum works until it doesn't — buy highs with volume confirmation and stop-losses, never on hope. Breakdowns deserve even stricter exits.

short: Exchange-traded fund: a basket of stocks, bonds or gold bought like one share. Instant diversification, tiny fees.
definition: An ETF (exchange-traded fund) holds a basket — an index, gold, bonds — and trades on exchange like a stock, with live prices through the day (unlike mutual funds' once-daily NAV).
Costs run far below active funds, but check tracking error (does it mirror its target?) and liquidity (can you exit at fair spreads?).
example: One Nifty 50 ETF unit gives you all fifty large-caps for under 0.1% yearly — diversification that once needed lakhs and a broker's patience.
inExtension: ETFs sit naturally in watchlists and the tape: track GoldBeES beside GLD, or Nifty ETFs beside the index, with alerts on each.

faqs.q: ETF vs mutual fund — which is better?
faqs.a: ETFs win on cost and intraday liquidity; index mutual funds win on SIP automation. Many investors hold both.

short: A rule-based basket measuring a market slice — Nifty 50, S&P 500, gold prices. The benchmark everything gets judged against.
definition: An index tracks a defined basket by fixed rules: membership criteria, weighting (usually market-cap) and review schedules. It turns 'the market' from a feeling into a number.
Indices power ETFs and index funds, benchmark active managers, and settle derivatives. Know an index's construction before concluding anything from its level.
example: Judging your 12% return? Against a Nifty at +8% you won; against Nasdaq-100 at +25% you chose the wrong arena. Benchmarks make returns honest.
inExtension: S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow and nine more economies' indices stream in the Markets tab with native currencies and macro context.

faqs.q: Can I buy an index directly?
faqs.a: No — buy its ETF or index fund shadow. Compare expense ratio and tracking error between shadows of the same index.

short: Initial public offering: a private company selling shares to the public first. Hype is high, history is short — screen harder.
definition: An IPO lists a company publicly via a price band, subscription window and allotment. Oversubscription makes headlines; fundamentals make returns.
New listings lack price history, so screen the prospectus: use of proceeds, promoter holding, anchor investors, and whether private-equity sellers are exiting at your entry price.
example: IPOs subscribed 100x+ on retail frenzy routinely list flat and drift for a year — demand for the paper exceeded demand for the business.
inExtension: Add IPO allotments to a dedicated portfolio the listing morning; price alerts catch the post-listing base forming while hype fades.

faqs.q: Are IPOs good investments?
faqs.a: Selectively. Established-profit IPOs at sane multiples compound; loss-making story IPOs at peak multiples mostly transfer wealth from public to promoters.

short: Current + savings account deposits — a bank's cheapest funding. Higher CASA means fatter margins and a stronger moat.
definition: CASA (current account + savings account) deposits cost banks ~3% versus ~7% for term deposits. A 45% CASA ratio structurally lowers funding cost and defends margins when rates rise.
Falling CASA industry-wide signals deposit wars: every bank pays more for funds, and net interest margins compress across the board.
example: Two banks with identical loan books: the 45%-CASA one earns ~0.5% extra margin yearly — compounding into a valuation gap within three years.
inExtension: Compare bank holdings on the switchable ROE column while reading CASA commentary in results — ratios plus narrative, one screen.

faqs.q: What CASA is good?
faqs.a: Above 40% is strong for large banks; SBI-scale CASA above 42% is exceptional. Trend matters more than a single quarter.

short: A fund's yearly fee as % of assets. A 1% fee silently eats a quarter of long-run gains — minimise it.
definition: The expense ratio is what ETFs and mutual funds charge yearly. Active equity funds take ~1–2%, index funds under ~0.3% — the gap compounds brutally over decades.
On a 12% gross return over 20 years, 2% fees versus 0.2% fees is the difference between ~9.6x and ~13.6x your money. Fees are the most reliable predictor of fund underperformance.
example: Two identical Nifty index funds at 0.05% and 0.30% fees diverge by lakhs on a crore-sized SIP over 15 years — for zero extra service.
inExtension: Screen your fund/ETF watchlist the same way you screen stocks: lowest fee among identical exposures usually wins.

faqs.q: Does expense ratio include exit load?
faqs.a: No — exit loads and taxes are separate. Total cost = expense ratio drag + loads + your tax on gains.

short: Confirmed-but-unexecuted contracts — future revenue already signed. The visibility metric for rail, defence and EPC stocks.
definition: An order book totals signed contracts awaiting execution. Divide it by yearly revenue ('book-to-bill' or coverage) to see how many years of work are already secured.
Quality beats size: government orders pay slowly but surely, private orders pay faster but cancel easier. Watch execution (conversion to revenue), not just addition.
example: A Rs 40,000-crore book on Rs 15,000-crore revenue = 2.7 years of visibility. If quarterly execution stalls, the book is decoration.
inExtension: Track order-heavy names across results season: tag them, watch execution quarters, and let alerts flag the breakout when numbers confirm.

faqs.q: Order book vs order inflow?
faqs.a: Inflow is new wins this period; book is the cumulative backlog. Inflow accelerates the story, book sustains it.

short: Bull = sustained +20% rise on optimism; bear = −20% fall on pessimism. Regimes decide strategy more than stock picks.
definition: A bull market rises 20%+ amid confidence, liquidity and earnings growth; a bear market falls 20%+ amid fear, tightening or recession. The labels describe sustained regimes, not single weeks.

Strategy follows regime: bulls reward buying dips and riding momentum; bears reward cash, quality balance sheets and staggered entries. Most investor damage comes from using bull tactics in bear markets.
example: 2020–21's liquidity bull forgave every mistake; 2022's rate-shock bear punished them. Same investors, opposite outcomes — regime did the work.
inExtension: Market Mood, breadth and heatmaps show regime shifts forming: narrowing breadth plus greed-zone mood has preceded most recent pullbacks.

faqs.q: Are we in a bull or bear market now?
faqs.a: Check the gauges, not gurus: index vs 200-day average, breadth trend, MMI/Fear-Greed zone. The extension surfaces all three live.
